newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - SAfrica Nov CPI seen edging nearer 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - SAfrica Nov CPI seen edging nearer 10 pct.

text.p: Rising food prices have once again been fingered as the culprit behind another expected rise in South African consumer inflation, with figures for November seen edging closer to double digits.
Economists said on Friday CPI data for December, due at 0900 GMT on Thursday, would edge higher in both November and December, with most predicting a peak in the first quarter of next year.

A Reuters poll of nine economists forecast the November consumer price index would increase by 9.5 percent year-on-year -- its highest level since July 1995 -- after a worse-than-expected 9.1 percent increase in October. The month-on-month increase was forecast at a robust 0.9 percent.
The range for the consensus was 9.2 to 9.8 percent.
"We are still seeing food prices under pressure. Meat prices have also increased in the run-up to Christmas," said Syfrets economist Sandra Gordon.

Food inflation jumped 12.4 percent year-on-year in October after a 10.4 percent increase in September. Economists blamed the upward trend on strong demand and heavy rains, which caused some supply problems.
But economists said food was not alone in heightening inflationary pressures in November as the prices of the whole basket of consumer goods had risen in the run-up to the Christmas season.
"Food is still a bit of a problem but basically it is coming from all across the board as we head towards the December shopping spree," said Nedcor Ltd economist Dennis Dykes.
A three cent hike in the price of gasoline during November and the lagged effects of the rand's depreciation against the dollar was also seen weighing on the figure.

But December's eight cent surge in gasoline prices was seen a strong factor in pushing up that month's inflation. Another weighty influence on the December figure would be the Reserve Bank's one percentage point hike in its key lending rate, economists said.
"We will see double digit inflation figures before the end of the year due to the November Bank rate increase," said Sanlam economist Pieter Calitz.
But others were more sanguine predicting inflation peaking at below 10 percent.
A poll of seven economists forecast inflation hitting a high of between 9.6 and 11 percent, with most expecting this to occur early next year in the months January to April.
However, a hike in VAT in the March 1997 national Budget could delay an expected downturn in inflation by several months, they said.
